sections.content: Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start, end]`, merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of non-overlapping intervals that cover all intervals in the input.
keyTakeaways: Sort intervals by start time first to enable linear single-pass merging.
Overlaps occur when the next interval's start time is less than or equal to the current interval's end time.

codeExample.title: Interval Sorting and Merging
codeExample.explanation: After sorting by start time, we iterate through intervals. If the current interval start is <= the previous interval end, we merge by expanding the previous end time; otherwise, we append the interval as a new non-overlapping range.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the time complexity of the Merge Intervals algorithm?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Sorting the interval array takes O(N log N) time, which dominates the linear O(N) single-pass iteration.

sections.title: Q27: Insert Interval
sections.content: You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start time and a `newInterval`. Insert `newInterval` into the intervals such that the list remains sorted and non-overlapping.
keyTakeaways: Process non-overlapping intervals before the new interval, merge all overlapping ones, then append remaining non-overlapping intervals.
Can be solved in a single O(N) linear pass without explicit full re-sorting.

codeExample.title: Linear Insert and Merge Interval
codeExample.explanation: Splits the process into three distinct phases: collecting left disjoint intervals, iteratively updating the min start and max end of overlapping bounds, and collecting right disjoint intervals.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is explicit array sorting not required for the Insert Interval algorithm?
options: Because input intervals are guaranteed to be sorted by start time initially
Because merge operations handle sorting automatically
Because intervals are stored in a binary heap
Because Javascript array push maintains sorted order
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The input interval array is pre-sorted, allowing linear O(N) partitioning around `newInterval`.

sections.title: Q28: Non-overlapping Intervals
sections.content: Given an array of intervals `intervals`, find the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping.
keyTakeaways: Greedy strategy: sort intervals by end time to preserve maximum remaining space.
Always pick the interval with the earliest end time to minimize collisions with future intervals.

codeExample.title: Greedy End-Time Interval Removal
codeExample.explanation: Sorting by end times allows greedily keeping intervals that finish earliest. If the next interval starts before `prevEnd`, it must be removed to prevent overlap.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why do we sort by end time rather than start time for greedy interval scheduling?
options: Choosing intervals that finish earliest leaves maximum possible remaining room for future intervals
Sorting by start time requires O(N²) time
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Selecting intervals that complete earliest maximizes available window space for remaining candidate intervals.

sections.title: Q29: Top K Frequent Elements
sections.content: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the $k$ most frequent elements. Solve it in $O(n)$ time using Bucket Sort.
keyTakeaways: Bucket Sort groups elements into array indices matching their exact frequency count.
Achieves $O(n)$ linear time complexity, beating $O(n \log n)$ heap/sorting methods.

codeExample.title: Bucket Sort Top K Frequent
codeExample.explanation: Counts occurrences in a Map, uses array indices as frequency buckets, and iterates backward from maximum possible frequency to extract top k items.

interactiveQuiz.question: What determines the size of the buckets array in this Bucket Sort implementation?
options: nums.length + 1 (the maximum possible frequency of any element)
The maximum number value in nums
interactiveQuiz.explanation: An element can appear at most `nums.length` times, so allocating `nums.length + 1` buckets safely indexes all possible frequencies.

sections.title: Q30: Encode and Decode Strings
sections.content: Design an algorithm to encode a list of strings to a single string and decode that single string back to the original list of strings.
keyTakeaways: Prefix each string with its character length followed by a delimiter (e.g. `4#code`).
Avoids parsing errors caused by delimiter characters appearing inside original string content.

codeExample.title: Length-Prefix String Serialization
codeExample.explanation: Encoding formats strings as `length#string`. Decoding locates `#`, parses integer `length`, and slices exact character byte segments safely.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is length-prefixing preferable to simple character delimiting (e.g. comma separation)?
options: Because comma characters can exist inside original strings and break simple split algorithms
Length-prefixing works only with ASCII characters
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If a string contains the delimiter (e.g. `,`), simple splitting corrupts the string boundary; length-prefixing guarantees fixed byte slicing.

sections.title: Q31: Longest Consecutive Sequence
sections.content: Given an unsorted array of integers `nums`, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence in $O(n)$ time.
keyTakeaways: Store numbers in a Hash Set to perform $O(1)$ presence lookups.
Only attempt to build sequences from the start of a sequence (`!set.has(num - 1)`).

codeExample.title: Hash Set Sequence Detection
codeExample.explanation: Converts array to Set. Loops through set, identifying sequence starters (`num - 1` missing). From starters, increments `currentNum` upward, measuring sequence length in $O(n)$ overall operations.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why does the inner while loop not degrade the algorithm time complexity to O(N²)?
options: Because the inner loop runs only for sequence starting elements, visiting each overall number at most twice
Because Set.has takes O(log N) time
Because set iteration sorts elements automatically
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Only numbers that start sequences enter the inner while loop, guaranteeing linear $O(N)$ execution total.

sections.title: Q32: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
sections.content: Given a sorted array of unique elements rotated between 1 and $n$ times, find the minimum element in $O(\log n)$ time using Binary Search.
keyTakeaways: Compare `nums[mid]` against `nums[right]` to determine which half is sorted.
If `nums[mid] > nums[right]`, minimum lies strictly in the right partition.

codeExample.title: Rotated Array Binary Search Minimum
codeExample.explanation: If `nums[mid] > nums[right]`, pivot point and minimum element must be right of mid (`left = mid + 1`). Otherwise minimum is at mid or left of mid (`right = mid`).

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is `right = mid` used instead of `right = mid - 1` when `nums[mid] <= nums[right]`?
options: Because `nums[mid]` itself could be the minimum element
interactiveQuiz.explanation: When `nums[mid] <= nums[right]`, `nums[mid]` might be the minimum value, so mid must be retained within search space bounds.

sections.title: Q33: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
sections.content: Given a rotated sorted array and a target integer, return its index or `-1` if not found in $O(\log n)$ time using modified Binary Search.
keyTakeaways: At least one partition half (`left..mid` or `mid..right`) is guaranteed to be sorted at any binary search step.
Check if target falls within sorted half boundaries to decide search direction.

codeExample.title: Rotated Sorted Array Search
codeExample.explanation: Identifies which half is sorted. If target lies within bounds of the sorted half, moves search space into that range; otherwise shifts into opposite partition.

interactiveQuiz.question: What structural guarantee enables binary search on a rotated sorted array?
options: At every step, at least one half of the partition array remains strictly sorted
The array length is always even
The target value is always near mid
Rotation moves all elements into reverse order
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Splitting a rotated sorted array in half always produces at least one completely sorted subarray partition.

sections.title: Q34: Reorder Linked List
sections.content: Reorder a singly linked list $L_0 \to L_1 \to \dots \to L_{n-1} \to L_n$ into $L_0 \to L_n \to L_1 \to L_{n-1} \to L_2 \to L_{n-2} \dots$ in-place.
keyTakeaways: 1) Find middle using Fast/Slow pointers. 2) Reverse second half. 3) Interleave nodes from both halves.
Performs transformation in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

codeExample.title: In-Place Linked List Interleaving
codeExample.explanation: Finds middle using slow/fast pointers, splits list, reverses second half, and weaves node pointers alternating between first and second sublists.

interactiveQuiz.question: What three sub-algorithms are combined to solve the Reorder List problem in-place?
options: Find Middle (Fast/Slow), Reverse Linked List, and Merge Interleaving
Binary Search, QuickSelect, and Breadth-First Search
Topological Sort, DFS, and Hash Map lookup
Kadane's Algorithm, Sliding Window, and Stack Pop
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Combining middle finding, second-half pointer reversal, and alternating node interleaving solves the problem in $O(1)$ auxiliary space.

sections.title: Q35: Remove Nth Node From End of List
sections.content: Given the head of a linked list, remove the $n$-th node from the end of the list and return its head in a single pass.
keyTakeaways: Use Two Pointers (`fast` and `slow`) offset by $n$ steps.
When `fast` reaches the list end, `slow` points directly before the target node to delete.

codeExample.title: Two-Pointer Offset Node Removal
codeExample.explanation: Advances `fast` $n+1$ steps ahead. Moving both pointers at equal speed keeps `slow` exactly $n$ steps behind `fast`. When `fast` reaches `null`, `slow.next = slow.next.next` deletes target.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is a dummy node initialized before the head of the linked list?
options: To safely handle cases where the head node itself must be removed
To convert the list into a circular structure
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If $n$ equals list length, the head node must be deleted; `dummy.next` seamlessly handles returning updated head node references.

sections.title: Q36: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
sections.content: Given a Binary Search Tree (BST), find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) node of two given nodes `p` and `q`.
keyTakeaways: Exploit BST properties: if both values are smaller than root, LCA lies in left subtree; if larger, in right subtree.
The split node where `p` and `q` diverge to opposite sides is the LCA.

codeExample.title: BST Lowest Common Ancestor Iterative Search
codeExample.explanation: Traverses tree using BST value properties. If both values are less than `curr.val`, move left. If both are greater, move right. Otherwise `curr` is the LCA.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the time complexity of LCA search on a balanced Binary Search Tree?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: On a balanced BST, traversing down node tree height takes logarithmic $O(\log N)$ operations.

sections.title: Q37: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
sections.content: Implement a Trie with `insert`, `search`, and `startsWith` methods for efficient string retrieval.
keyTakeaways: Tree data structure where nodes represent individual character character branches.
Enables $O(m)$ string insertions and prefix lookups where $m$ is string length.

codeExample.title: Trie Prefix Tree Implementation
codeExample.explanation: Nodes contain a child map and end-of-word boolean. Character insertions create tree branches; searches follow character edges step by step.

interactiveQuiz.question: What differentiates search(word) from startsWith(prefix) in a Trie?
options: search verifies that the node reached has `isEndOfWord = true`
startsWith works only on root nodes
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `search` requires the final node to complete a full word (`isEndOfWord = true`), whereas `startsWith` accepts any matching prefix node.

sections.title: Q38: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
sections.content: Design a data structure supporting adding words and searching words, where the '.' character can match any single letter.
keyTakeaways: Combines Trie storage with DFS recursion when encountering wildcard `.` characters.
Wildcard `.` branches out to search all available children nodes at current tree depth.

codeExample.title: Trie Wildcard Search Engine
codeExample.explanation: Extends basic Trie structure. If search character is `.`, loops through all child branches recursively; otherwise follows standard character branch.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does the search algorithm process a wildcard '.' character during DFS?
options: Iterates through every valid child key at current node, recursively attempting matches
Converts '.' into an ASCII space character
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Wildcards match any character, forcing DFS to evaluate all existing child branch paths for that level.

sections.title: Q39: Subsets (Power Set Backtracking)
sections.content: Given an integer array `nums` of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set) using Backtracking.
keyTakeaways: Generates $2^n$ total subsets.
Backtracking pattern: 1) Include choice, 2) Recurse, 3) Pop choice (backtrack).

codeExample.title: Backtracking Power Set Generator
codeExample.explanation: Saves candidate array snapshot at every recursion step, iterates choices from current index, pushes choice, recurses, and pops choice to explore state options.

interactiveQuiz.question: How many total subsets exist for a set containing N unique elements?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Each element has two options (include or exclude), resulting in $2^N$ total power set subsets.

sections.title: Q40: Combination Sum
sections.content: Given an array of distinct integers `candidates` and a `target`, return all unique combinations where candidate numbers sum to target. Numbers can be reused infinitely.
keyTakeaways: Backtracking recursion allows reusing current number by passing index `i` instead of `i + 1`.
Prunes exploration branches when `remain < 0`.

codeExample.title: Unbounded Choice Combination Sum
codeExample.explanation: Prunes search when `remain < 0`. When `remain === 0`, saves combination. Reuses element by passing `i` to recursive call.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is the index parameter `i` passed to recursive backtrack(remain - candidates[i], current, i) instead of `i + 1`?
options: To permit reusing the same candidate number unlimited times in a combination
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Passing index `i` retains current number access for subsequent branch steps, allowing infinite element reuse.

sections.title: Q41: House Robber (Dynamic Programming)
sections.content: Find the maximum money you can rob tonight without alerting police (cannot rob adjacent houses).
keyTakeaways: State transition: $dp[i] = \max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + \text{nums}[i])$.
Optimizable to O(1) space tracking two previous max values (`rob1`, `rob2`).

codeExample.title: DP House Robber O(1) Space
codeExample.explanation: At house `n`, compares robbing current house plus max from two houses prior (`n + rob1`) against max from previous house (`rob2`). Shifts window values forward.

interactiveQuiz.question: What constraint prevents taking the simple sum of all array elements in House Robber?
options: Adjacent houses cannot be robbed on the same night
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Robbing adjacent houses triggers security alarms, requiring choice between house $i-1$ vs house $i-2 + \text{current}$.

sections.title: Q42: House Robber II (Circular DP)
sections.content: All houses are arranged in a circle. Find max stolen money given adjacent houses cannot be robbed.
keyTakeaways: Circular arrangement implies first house and last house are adjacent and cannot both be robbed.
Run standard House Robber algorithm twice: range `0..n-2` and range `1..n-1`, taking maximum result.

codeExample.title: Circular House Robber Solution
codeExample.explanation: Splits problem into two linear sub-problems: excluding the last house (`0..n-2`) vs excluding the first house (`1..n-1`), returning whichever yield is higher.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does House Robber II handle the circular house arrangement constraint?
options: Runs linear House Robber twice: once excluding the first house and once excluding the last house
interactiveQuiz.explanation: First and last houses cannot both be chosen; evaluating subsets excluding either first or last resolves the circular conflict.

sections.title: Q43: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)
sections.content: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence in an integer array.
keyTakeaways: Standard Dynamic Programming approach takes $O(n^2)$ time.
Patience Sorting with Binary Search optimizes LIS execution to $O(n \log n)$ time.

codeExample.title: Patience Sort Binary Search LIS O(n log n)
codeExample.explanation: Maintains array `tails` storing smallest tail values of increasing subsequences. For each `num`, uses binary search to replace smallest element >= `num` or append `num` if larger than all tails.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the time complexity of the Patience Sorting Binary Search LIS algorithm?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Iterating $n$ items and performing binary search per item takes $O(n \log n)$ time.

sections.title: Q44: Palindromic Substrings (Expand Around Center)
sections.content: Given a string `s`, return the count of palindromic substrings in `s` using Expand Around Center method.
keyTakeaways: Consider $2n - 1$ possible expansion centers (odd single characters and even adjacent character pairs).
Achieves $O(n^2)$ time and $O(1)$ space complexity.

codeExample.title: Center Expansion Palindrome Counter
codeExample.explanation: Iterates every character index, expanding outward for odd-length palindromes (`i, i`) and even-length palindromes (`i, i+1`), incrementing counts while characters match.

interactiveQuiz.question: How many total potential palindrome centers exist for a string of length N?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: There are $N$ single character centers and $N-1$ adjacent pair centers, totaling $2N-1$ centers.

sections.title: Q45: Longest Palindromic Substring
sections.content: Given a string `s`, return the longest palindromic substring in `s` using Expand Around Center approach.
keyTakeaways: Expands around odd and even centers while keeping track of max substring bounds.
Runs in $O(n^2)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space.

codeExample.title: Center Expansion Longest Palindrome
codeExample.explanation: Expands outward from odd and even center indices. When expansion breaks, calculates valid length (`right - left - 1`) and updates best `start` index and `maxLength`.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of the Expand Around Center method for Longest Palindromic Substring?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Tracking only indices (`start`, `maxLength`, `left`, `right`) uses constant $O(1)$ space.

sections.title: Q46: Word Break (Dynamic Programming)
sections.content: Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be segmented into space-separated dictionary words.
keyTakeaways: Boolean array `dp[i]` represents if prefix `s[0..i]` can be segmented.
State transition: `dp[i] = dp[j] && wordDict.has(s[j..i])` for $0 \le j < i$.

codeExample.title: DP String Segmentation Word Break
codeExample.explanation: `dp[i]` is true if there exists split index $j$ where `dp[j]` is true and substring `s[j..i]` is present in `wordSet`.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does dp[i] = true signify in the Word Break dynamic programming array?
options: The substring prefix s.substring(0, i) can be validly partitioned into dictionary words
The character s[i] is a vowel
The string ends at index i
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `dp[i]` tracks segmentability for prefix string length $i$ starting from index 0.

sections.title: Q47: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow (Graph Multi-Source DFS)
sections.content: Find grid coordinate cells where rain water can flow to both Pacific (top/left) and Atlantic (bottom/right) oceans.
keyTakeaways: Reverse flow simulation: DFS outward from ocean boundaries upstream to reachable higher/equal elevation land cells.
Cells reachable by both Pacific DFS and Atlantic DFS are valid answer coordinates.

codeExample.title: Reverse Flow Boundary DFS
codeExample.explanation: Runs DFS backward from Pacific edges and Atlantic edges upstream (heights[r][c] >= prevHeight). Cells marked true in both boolean grids are returned.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why does the algorithm perform DFS backward from ocean boundaries instead of forward from every cell?
options: Prevents redundant overlapping search evaluations, dropping complexity from O(rows² * cols²) down to O(rows * cols)
Because water flows upward in graph matrices
Forward DFS causes call stack overflow
To avoid using boolean visited matrices
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Starting at ocean borders requires traversing cells at most twice overall ($O(R \times C)$ time), whereas probing each cell forward causes massive re-computations.

sections.title: Q48: Sum of Two Integers (Bitwise Logic)
sections.content: Calculate the sum of two integers `a` and `b` without using the operators `+` and `-`.
keyTakeaways: XOR operator (`^`) calculates sum without carry.
AND operator (`&`) followed by bitwise left shift (`<< 1`) calculates carry values.

codeExample.title: Bitwise Addition
codeExample.explanation: `a & b` finds matching bit carries, shifted left by 1. `a ^ b` calculates half-adder sum. Process repeats until carry `b` becomes 0.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which bitwise operator computes binary addition without handling carry bits?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: XOR (`^`) performs binary addition for bit pairs ($1^1 = 0, 1^0 = 1, 0^0 = 0$), acting as a half-adder without carry.

sections.title: Q49: Number of 1 Bits (Hamming Weight)
sections.content: Write a function that takes an unsigned integer and returns the number of '1' bits it has (Hamming Weight).
keyTakeaways: Brian Kernighan's bit manipulation trick `n = n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit in $O(1)$ operations per set bit.
Loop iterations match the exact count of set bits rather than iterating all 32 bit positions.

codeExample.title: Brian Kernighan Bit Clearing Algorithm
codeExample.explanation: Evaluating `n & (n - 1)` drops the rightmost set bit (`1`) to `0` in each step, incrementing `count` until all set bits are cleared.

interactiveQuiz.question: What effect does executing the bitwise operation `n & (n - 1)` have on binary integer `n`?
options: Flips the lowest set bit (rightmost 1) to 0
Shifts all bits left by 1 position
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `n & (n - 1)` clears the least significant set bit (`1`), providing $O(\text{set bits})$ counting performance.

sections.title: Q50: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
sections.content: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree into a single string and deserialize that string back into the original binary tree structure.
keyTakeaways: Pre-order traversal DFS converts tree to comma-separated string, using sentinel tokens (e.g. `'N'`) for null nodes.
Deserialization reconstructs nodes sequentially from queue tokens.

codeExample.title: Pre-Order DFS Tree Serialization
codeExample.explanation: `serialize` performs pre-order DFS adding node values or 'N' for nulls into a CSV string. `deserialize` consumes tokens sequentially, creating node objects recursively.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why are explicit null markers ('N') required in pre-order tree serialization?
options: To preserve exact tree structure so deserialization can uniquely rebuild subtrees without ambiguity
To mark leaf nodes for memory deallocation
Required for JSON string syntax rules
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Including null leaf markers ensures pre-order token sequences uniquely describe tree node relationships without ambiguity.
